72:                PrintStream::class.java

74:            runner::class.java.getMethod("execute").invoke(runner)
75:        } catch (reflectionWrapper: InvocationTargetException) {
76:            processResult(reflectionWrapper.targetException.message, reflectionWrapper, ignoreFailures)

14:    private val classpathFilesHashWithLoaders = ConcurrentHashMap<Int, URLClassLoader>()

23:        }
24:    }

28:                .map { DefaultAnalysisResult(emptyContainer()) }
29:                .getOrElse { DefaultAnalysisResult(null, UnexpectedError(it)) }
30:        } else {
31:            Runner(arguments, outputChannel, errorChannel).call()

10:internal class MissingRulesConfigValidator(private val baseline: YamlConfig, private val excludePatterns: Set<Regex>) :
11:    AbstractYamlConfigValidator() {
12:
13:    override val id: String = "MissingRulesConfigValidator"
14:
15:    override fun validate(configToValidate: YamlConfig, settings: ValidationSettings): Collection<Notification> {
16:        if (!settings.checkExhaustiveness) {
17:            return emptyList()
18:        }
19:        return ruleSetNames.flatMap { ruleSet -> validateRuleSet(ruleSet, configToValidate) }
20:    }
21:
22:    private fun validateRuleSet(ruleSet: RuleSetId, configToValidate: YamlConfig): List<Notification> {
23:        val ruleSetConfigToValidate = configToValidate.getSubMapOrNull(ruleSet)
24:        val ruleSetConfigFromBaseline = baseline.getSubMapOrNull(ruleSet)
25:        return when {
26:            ruleSetConfigFromBaseline == null -> emptyList()
27:            ruleSetConfigToValidate == null -> listOf(ruleSetMissing(ruleSet))
28:            else -> checkForMissingRules(ruleSet, ruleSetConfigToValidate, ruleSetConfigFromBaseline)
29:        }
30:    }
31:
32:    private fun checkForMissingRules(
33:        ruleSetName: RuleSetId,
34:        ruleSetConfigToValidate: Map<String, Any>,
35:        ruleSetConfigFromBaseline: Map<String, Any>,
36:    ): List<Notification> {
37:        if (ruleSetConfigToValidate[Config.ACTIVE_KEY] == false) {
38:            return emptyList()
39:        }
40:
41:        return ruleSetConfigFromBaseline.keys
42:            .filter { ruleNameCandidate -> excludePatterns.none { it.matches("$ruleSetName>$ruleNameCandidate") } }
43:            .filter { ruleName -> !ruleSetConfigToValidate.containsKey(ruleName) }
44:            .map { ruleName -> ruleMissing(ruleName, ruleSetName) }
45:    }
46:
47:    private fun ruleMissing(ruleName: String, ruleSetName: RuleSetId): Notification =
48:        Notification(
49:            "Rule '$ruleName' from the '$ruleSetName' rule set is missing in the configuration.",
50:            Notification.Level.Warning,
51:        )
52:
53:    private fun ruleSetMissing(ruleSetName: RuleSetId): Notification =
54:        Notification(
55:            "Rule set '$ruleSetName' is missing in the configuration.",
56:            Notification.Level.Warning,
57:        )

To add constructor calls you need to define them with `<init>`, for example `java.util.Date.<init>`. To add calls involving type parameters, omit them, for example `fun hello(args: Array<Any>)` is referred to as simply `hello(kotlin.Array)`. To add calls involving varargs, for example `fun hello(vararg args: String)`, you need to define it like `hello(vararg String)`. website\versioned_docs\version-2.0.0-alpha.3\rules\style.mdx:1065:  List of fully qualified method signatures which are forbidden. Methods can be defined without full signature (i.e. `java.time.LocalDate.now`) which will report calls of all methods with this name or with full signature (i.e. `java.time.LocalDate(java.time.Clock)`) which would report only call with this concrete signature. If you want to forbid an extension function like `fun String.hello(a: Int)` you should add the receiver parameter as the first parameter like this: `hello(kotlin.String, kotlin.Int)`. To forbid constructor calls you need to define them with `<init>`, for example `java.util.Date.<init>`. To forbid calls involving type parameters, omit them, for example `fun hello(args: Array<Any>)` is referred to as simply `hello(kotlin.Array)`. To forbid calls involving varargs for example `fun hello(vararg args: String)` you need to define it like `hello(vararg String)`. To forbid methods from the companion object reference the Companion class, for example as `TestClass.Companion.hello()` (even if it is marked `@JvmStatic`). To match function type parameters like `initializer` in `fun <T> lazy(initializer: () -> T)`, use `kotlin.Function{N}` where N is the number of parameters the function takes. For example, `kotlin.lazy(kotlin.Function0)` matches calls to `lazy { ... }`.

Methods can be defined without full signature (i.e. `java.time.LocalDate.now`) which will report calls of all methods with this name or with full signature (i.e. `java.time.LocalDate(java.time.Clock)`) which would report only call with this concrete signature. If you want to forbid an extension function like `fun String.hello(a: Int)` you should add the receiver parameter as the first parameter like this: `hello(kotlin.String, kotlin.Int)`. To forbid constructor calls you need to define them with `<init>`, for example `java.util.Date.<init>`. To forbid calls involving type parameters, omit them, for example `fun hello(args: Array<Any>)` is referred to as simply `hello(kotlin.Array)` (also the signature for vararg parameters). To forbid methods from the companion object reference the Companion class, for example as `TestClass.Companion.hello()` (even if it is marked `@JvmStatic`).

Methods can be defined without full signature (i.e. `java.time.LocalDate.now`) which will report calls of all methods with this name or with full signature (i.e. `java.time.LocalDate(java.time.Clock)`) which would report only call with this concrete signature. If you want to forbid an extension function like `fun String.hello(a: Int)` you should add the receiver parameter as the first parameter like this: `hello(kotlin.String, kotlin.Int)`. To forbid constructor calls you need to define them with `<init>`, for example `java.util.Date.<init>`. To forbid calls involving type parameters, omit them, for example `fun hello(args: Array<Any>)` is referred to as simply `hello(kotlin.Array)` (also the signature for vararg parameters). Detekt offers a compiler plugin for K1 which allows you to run detekt as part of the Kotlin compilation process using [type resolution](type-resolution.mdx). This allows you to run detekt on your code without having separate tasks to invoke and results in much faster execution of detekt, especially if you use type resolution with the Gradle plugin. 12: 13::::caution 14: 15:Please note that Detekt Compiler Plugin is an **experimental extension** of detekt. We expect it to be stable with the upcoming release of detekt (2.x) 16: 17:::: 18: 19:## Using Gradle 20: 21:### Adding the Compiler Plugin 22: 23:To use the detekt Compiler Plugin, you will have to add the following Gradle Plugin: 24: 25:```kotlin 26:plugins { 27: id("io.github.detekt.gradle.compiler-plugin") version "[detekt_version]" 28:} 29:``` 30: 31:### Configuring the Compiler Plugin 32: 33:The compiler plugin can be configured using the `detekt {}` block in your gradle file. 34: 35:The following options are allowed: 36: 37:```kotlin 38:detekt { 39: // Define the detekt configuration(s) you want to use. 40: // Defaults to the default detekt configuration. 41: config.setFrom("path/to/config.yml") 42: 43: // Applies the config files on top of detekt's default config file. `false` by default. 44: buildUponDefaultConfig = false 45: 46: // Turns on all the rules. `false` by default. 47: allRules = false 48: 49: // Specifying a baseline file. All findings stored in this file in subsequent runs of detekt. 50: baseline = file("path/to/baseline.xml") 51: 52: // Disables all default detekt rulesets and will only run detekt with custom rules 53: // defined in plugins passed in with `detektPlugins` configuration. `false` by default. 54: disableDefaultRuleSets = false 55: 56: // Adds debug output during task execution. `false` by default. 57: debug = false 58: 59: // Kill switch to turn off the Compiler Plugin execution entirely. 60: enableCompilerPlugin.set(true) 61:} 62:``` 63: 64:Moreover, detekt reports can be configured at the Kotlin Compilation tasks level as follows 65: 66:```kotlin 67:tasks.withType(org.jetbrains.kotlin.gradle.tasks.KotlinCompile).configureEach { 68: detekt { 69: reports { 70: checkstyle.enabled.set(true) 71: markdown.enabled.set(false) 72: create("custom") { 73: enabled.set(false) 74: } 75: } 76: } 77:} 78:``` 79: 80:### Adding third party plugins 81: 82:As for the Detekt Gradle Plugin, you can add third party plugins to the Compiler Plugin using the `detektPlugins` configuration. 83: 84:```kotlin 85:dependencies { 86: detektPlugins("dev.detekt:detekt-rules-ktlint-wrapper:[detekt_version]") 87:} 88:``` 89: 90:### Running the Compiler Plugin 91: 92:The compiler plugin will run during your `compileKotlin` tasks execution: 93: 94:```shell 95:$ ./gradlew compileKotlin 96: 97:> Task :example:compileKotlin 98:w: Analysis failed with 1 issues. 99:w: file:///.../example/src/main/java/Sample.kt:4:17 MagicNumber: This expression contains a magic number. 252:## Integrating extensions with detekt {/* #configureextensions */}
253:
254:So you have implemented your own rules or other extensions and want to integrate them
255:into your `detekt` run? Great, make sure to have a `jar` with all your needed dependencies 
256:minus the ones `detekt` brings itself.
257:
258:Take a look at our [sample project](https://github.com/detekt/detekt/tree/main/detekt-sample-extensions) on how to achieve this with gradle.
259:
260:### Via the Detekt CLI
261:
262:Pass your `jar` with the `--plugins` flag when calling the CLI fatjar:
263:```sh
264:detekt --input ... --plugins /path/to/my/jar
265:```
266:
267:### Via the Detekt Gradle Plugin
268:
269:For example `detekt` itself provides a wrapper over [ktlint](https://github.com/pinterest/ktlint) as a 
270:custom rule set. To enable it, we add the published dependency to `detekt` via the `detektPlugins` configuration:
271:
272:```kotlin
273:dependencies {
274:    detektPlugins("dev.detekt:detekt-rules-ktlint-wrapper:[detekt_version]")
275:}
276:```
277:
278:You can use the same method to apply any other custom rulesets! See the [Detekt 3rd-party Marketplace](https://detekt.dev/marketplace) for more.
279:
280:### Pitfalls
281:
282:- All rules are disabled by default and have to be explicitly enabled in the `detekt` yaml configuration file.
283:- If your extension is part of your project and you integrate it like `detektPlugins(project(":my-rules"))` make sure that this
284:subproject is built before `gradle detekt` is run.
285:In the `kotlin-dsl` you could add something like `tasks.withType<Detekt> { dependsOn(":my-rules:assemble") }` to explicitly run `detekt` only 
286:after your extension subproject is built.
287:- If you use detekt for your Android project and if you want to integrate all your custom rules in a new module, please make sure that
288:you put them in a pure kotlin module with no Android dependencies. `kotlin("jvm")` is enough to make it work.
289:- Sometimes when you run detekt task, you may not see the violations detected by your custom rules. In this case open a terminal and run
290:`./gradlew --stop` to stop gradle daemons and run the task again.
291:- If you are configuring a custom detekt task at the root project level, you will need to apply the detektPlugins at the root project as well (not subprojects). See [this issue](https://github.com/detekt/detekt/issues/3989#issuecomment-890331512) for more.

34:    fun analyze(): Detektion {

36:        val filesToAnalyze = measure(Phase.Parsing) { settings.ktFiles }
37:        if (settings.spec.projectSpec.analysisMode == AnalysisMode.full) {
38:            measure(Phase.ValidateClasspath) { validateClasspath(filesToAnalyze) }
39:        }
40:        val analysisMode = settings.spec.projectSpec.analysisMode
41:        val (processors, rules) = measure(Phase.LoadingExtensions) {
42:            val rules = getRules(
43:                analysisMode = analysisMode,
44:                ruleSetProviders = ruleSetsProvider.invoke(),
45:                config = settings.config,
46:                log = settings::debug,
47:            )
48:            processorsProvider.invoke() to rules
49:        }

51:        val result = measure(Phase.Analyzer) {
52:            val analyzer = Analyzer(settings, rules.filter { it.ruleInstance.active }, processors, analysisMode)
53:            processors.forEach { it.onStart(filesToAnalyze) }
54:            val issues = analyzer.run(filesToAnalyze)
55:            val detektion = Detektion(issues, rules.map { it.ruleInstance })
56:            processors.fold(detektion) { acc, processor -> processor.onFinish(filesToAnalyze, acc) }

74:                        getLineAndColumnRangeInPsiFile(diagnostic.psi.containingFile, diagnostic.psi.textRange)

76:                    val location = CompilerMessageLocationWithRange.create(
77:                        diagnostic.psi.containingFile.virtualFile.path,
78:                        lineAndColumnRange.start.line,
79:                        lineAndColumnRange.start.column,
80:                        lineAndColumnRange.end.line,
81:                        lineAndColumnRange.end.column,
82:                        lineAndColumnRange.start.lineContent

31:                    val fail = checkFailurePolicy(detektion)

## Conclusion

Assuming the CLI and Gradle runs use the same detekt version and effective YAML settings, responsibility most likely lies in the Gradle plugin’s invocation/classloader boundary—not in third-party `RuleSetProvider` discovery or core rule configuration.

The Gradle task ultimately invokes the same `dev.detekt.cli.Main.buildRunner` used by the CLI, but it supplies plugins differently: CLI plugin JARs become explicit extension paths, whereas Gradle puts them into a globally cached execution classloader and passes no `--plugins` argument (detekt-gradle-plugin/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/gradle/invoke/DetektInvoker.kt:61-74, detekt-gradle-plugin/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/gradle/Detekt.kt:172-206, detekt-gradle-plugin/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/gradle/Detekt.kt:218-239).

## Verified current behavior

- `detektPlugins` is a resolvable, transitive Gradle configuration, and it becomes each task’s `pluginClasspath` (detekt-gradle-plugin/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/gradle/plugin/DetektBasePlugin.kt:59-65, detekt-gradle-plugin/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/gradle/plugin/DetektPlugin.kt:137-171).
- The CLI’s supported contract is `--plugins`; parsing records those JAR paths in `CliArgs.plugins`, and `createSpec` installs them with `extensions.fromPaths` (detekt-cli/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/cli/CliArgs.kt:78-85, detekt-cli/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/cli/Spec.kt:62-65).
- The Gradle analysis task does not create a plugin argument. Its argument list includes input, compiler, configuration, rules, and report options, but not `pluginClasspath` (detekt-gradle-plugin/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/gradle/Detekt.kt:172-206). Instead, both execution modes combine `detektClasspath` and `pluginClasspath` into the classpath passed to `DefaultCliInvoker` (detekt-gradle-plugin/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/gradle/Detekt.kt:218-239).
- Curiously, Gradle’s debug-only reproduction command displays `pluginClasspath` as `--plugins`, even though actual execution does not use that argument (detekt-gradle-plugin/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/gradle/Detekt.kt:243-255). This is strong evidence that CLI-equivalent plugin-path semantics are intended.
- Core service discovery loads `RuleSetProvider` implementations from `ProcessingSettings.pluginLoader` (detekt-core/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/core/rules/RuleSets.kt:11-13). Explicit extension paths create a dedicated `URLClassLoader`, parented by detekt’s classloader, which is closed after processing; absent explicit paths, core falls back to its own classloader (detekt-core/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/core/settings/ClassloaderAware.kt:29-55).
- Plugin-provided `config/config.yml` resources are also read through that plugin loader, so selecting an old or wrong loader can affect both whether the provider exists and which defaults appear to configure it (detekt-core/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/core/tooling/DefaultConfigProvider.kt:32-45).
- Gradle’s execution loader is globally cached. Its key is only the integer hash code of the set of file paths; neither the full set nor file contents are retained in the key (detekt-gradle-plugin/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/gradle/internal/ClassLoaderCache.kt:12-27). Consequently:
  - distinct classpaths with colliding set hash codes can receive the wrong loader;
  - replacing a locally built plugin JAR at the same path can reuse a loader that has already loaded its old classes/resources.
- Existing cache tests verify path equality, path difference, and order independence, but do not cover hash collisions or replacement of a JAR at an unchanged path (detekt-gradle-plugin/src/test/kotlin/dev/detekt/gradle/internal/ClassLoaderCacheSpec.kt:14-39).

A clean-daemon, first-run failure is not explained merely by ServiceLoader: on the first execution the combined parent classloader should expose the plugin. In that case, first rule out input differences:

- Gradle automatically selects the root project’s `config/detekt/detekt.yml` when present (detekt-gradle-plugin/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/gradle/plugin/DetektBasePlugin.kt:53-57).
- Custom plugin defaults are merged when configuration is empty or `buildUponDefaultConfig` is enabled; a non-empty explicit configuration with that option disabled does not receive those defaults (detekt-core/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/core/tooling/ProcessingSpecSettingsBridge.kt:43-75).
- Rule activation is derived from the selected ruleset/rule subconfiguration, with individual rules inactive by default unless configuration activates them (detekt-core/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/core/RuleDescriptor.kt:30-74).

Thus, a CLI invocation without `--config` and a Gradle invocation that auto-selects a project YAML are not equivalent.

## Proposed fix boundary

The smallest robust boundary is the classic Gradle plugin’s argument/classloader assembly:

1. Add an internal `PluginsArgument` alongside `ConfigArgument`, serializing `pluginClasspath` with `File.pathSeparator`, matching the CLI splitter (detekt-gradle-plugin/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/gradle/invoke/CliArgument.kt:138-145, detekt-cli/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/cli/ArgumentConverters.kt:68-70).
2. Include it in analysis, baseline, and generate-config argument lists.
3. Pass only `detektClasspath` to `DefaultCliInvoker`; let core create and close the plugin loader through the existing `--plugins` path.
4. Apply the same separation in worker and non-worker branches. Baseline and config generation currently combine the two classpaths in the same way as analysis (detekt-gradle-plugin/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/gradle/DetektCreateBaselineTask.kt:187-206, detekt-gradle-plugin/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/gradle/DetektGenerateConfigTask.kt:49-71).

This confines the behavioral fix to `detekt-gradle-plugin`; core discovery, configuration merging, and the third-party API need no change. It also removes mutable third-party JARs from the global execution-loader cache.

If the implementation retains the combined-classpath design, the narrower fallback is to repair `DefaultClassLoaderCache`: use a collision-safe immutable classpath key and account for in-place content changes. Changing only `Int` to `Set<File>` fixes collisions but does not fix a rebuilt JAR at the same path, so it is insufficient for the full reported symptom.

## Verification plan

- Add argument unit tests for zero, one, and multiple plugin JARs, including Windows path-separator behavior.
- Add a TestKit fixture containing a minimal service-registered `RuleSetProvider` and `config/config.yml`. Run CLI and Gradle with the same source, YAML, flags, and detekt version; assert identical registered rulesets and findings. Debug logging already prints registered provider class names (detekt-core/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/core/rules/RuleSets.kt:34-38).
- In one long-lived Gradle daemon, run with plugin JAR version A, replace that same path with version B containing a distinguishable provider/rule/default configuration, and rerun. The second execution must observe B without `gradle --stop`.
- Exercise two projects/tasks with different plugin classpaths, including deliberately colliding Java file-set hash codes if the cache remains, and assert that neither task sees the other plugin.
- Parameterize functional coverage with `detekt.use.worker.api=false` and `true`, because the task has separate submission paths (detekt-gradle-plugin/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/gradle/Detekt.kt:218-239).
- Cover `detekt`, baseline creation, and config generation; config generation explicitly uses plugin paths to collect contributed defaults on the CLI path (detekt-cli/src/main/kotlin/dev/detekt/cli/runners/ConfigExporter.kt:8-18).
- Add configuration-control cases: explicit activation must run the rule; a non-empty YAML omitting it with `buildUponDefaultConfig=false` should remain inactive; enabling `buildUponDefaultConfig` should merge the plugin default. This prevents an expected configuration difference from being mistaken for a loading regression.

Documentation rationale, not proof of the defect: the extension guide requires a plugin JAR to omit dependencies supplied by detekt, says custom rules must be activated, and currently recommends stopping Gradle daemons when custom violations disappear (website/docs/introduction/extensions.mdx:252-290). After the loader fix is verified, that daemon-stop workaround should be removed or narrowed.
